articles.title: Kapso's Iterative Learning Loop: Enterprise Agents That Build Knowledge Graphs Without Retraining
articles.excerpt: Most enterprise AI agents treat knowledge as static. You embed documents, index them, and hope retrieval finds the right context. Kapso takes a different approach: it runs experiments against enterpri…
articles.body: Most enterprise AI agents treat knowledge as static. You embed documents, index them, and hope retrieval finds the right context. Kapso takes a different approach: it runs experiments against enterprise data, learns from the results, and updates a knowledge graph incrementally. No retraining cycles. No upfront ontology design. Just a feedback loop that compounds understanding across investigations. The architecture matters because enterprise data environments are messy. One of Kapso's reference projects involved migrating 30+ source systems, thousands of tables, and hundreds of BI reports to a lakehouse. No single person or agent understood how the estate connected.
articles.author: mech.app

articles.title: RAG Permissions at Retrieval Time: Why \\\\\\\"Don't Show It\\\\\\\" Fails as Agent Access Control
articles.excerpt: Tutorial RAG systems embed a folder and return the top five chunks. Production RAG systems embed a company with HR files, board decks, customer contracts, and incident reports where half the pages are…
articles.body: Tutorial RAG systems embed a folder and return the top five chunks. Production RAG systems embed a company with HR files, board decks, customer contracts, and incident reports where half the pages are restricted to specific teams. The moment multiple users with different permissions query the same index, you have an authorization problem that prompt instructions cannot solve. The most common mistake is trying to enforce access control in the prompt: You may only use documents the user is permitted to see. Do not reveal confidential information. By the time the model reads that instruction, the confidential chunk is already in its context window. You are asking a probabilistic text generator to un-know something you just handed it. Sometimes it complies.

articles.body: DDBD: the database behind Skapi, now free and open source on Linux and macOS Hello, and thank you for being here. Today we are releasing something we have been building toward since the first day of Skapi: DDBD , a schemaless record database with writer-based access control (WBAC). It is the record design that runs Skapi's database, packed into a server you can run yourself. It is free and open source under the Apache-2.0 license, and it runs on Linux and macOS. Everything about it is at ddbd.skapi.com . This article explains the problems we set out to solve from day one, how DDBD solves them, how it performs against PostgreSQL, MongoDB and SQLite, and how to install it in a minute.

articles.title: The Post-Quantum Transition, Protocol by Protocol: Your Pipelines and Your Agents
articles.excerpt: Almost every connection and credential in your data platform and your agents rests on RSA or elliptic-curve cryptography. On 27 October 2026 NIST published the final version of its plan for retiring b…
articles.body: Almost every connection and credential in your data platform and your agents rests on RSA or elliptic-curve cryptography. On 27 October 2026 NIST published the final version of its plan for retiring both. All quantum-vulnerable signature and key-establishment algorithms are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035 (NIST, 2026). In NIST's terms, deprecated means you may still use an algorithm but you carry some security risk in doing so; disallowed means you may no longer use it for that purpose (NIST, 2026). The 2030 step is the part that changed. According to a comparison of the two versions, the November 2024 draft deprecated only 112-bit parameter sets after 2030, such as RSA-2048 and P-224.
articles.author: Andrew Stevens

articles.body: We stream live sessions in many languages. One program can run in 20 or more languages over time: a few languages one week, a different set the next. Every program has several sessions (five, six, seven), and every session has its own set of media files, which we call a kit. Kits are updated all the time. For a long time we built the vMix preset for each session by hand. It worked, until it didn't. This post is about the two ways it failed and the small free tool we built so it can't fail that way again. If your team rebuilds a similar playlist for every event, you can reuse the method. Problem 1: vMix finds files by name Three teams touch every session. The content team prepares the material, the programs team arranges it into sessions, and the technical team supports the live stream.

articles.title: Testing offline Android translators with adb and airplane mode
articles.excerpt: Offline translation is one of those claims that's easy to make and annoying to verify. You tap a button, text appears, and you have no idea whether the phone quietly grabbed a mobile data connection b…
articles.body: Offline translation is one of those claims that's easy to make and annoying to verify. You tap a button, text appears, and you have no idea whether the phone quietly grabbed a mobile data connection behind your back. So I set up a small, repeatable test: same phone, same sentence, same target language, airplane mode on, and adb capturing the evidence as files instead of my memory of what I saw on screen. The two contenders were Google Translate (installed from Google Play) and InkPeek, a translator that runs an AI model locally on the device. The whole run takes about 25 minutes and sits at intermediate level, mostly because you drive the phone from a PC. One warning before we start: my source material doesn't state InkPeek's package name, minimum Android version, model size or price.

articles.body: While that was the first official Peanuts comic, a similar version by Charles Schulz predated Peanuts and ran in Minnesota’s St. Paul Pioneer Press. It was called Li’l Folks and also starred cute little children, although it did not have a regular cast like Peanuts would. Li’l Folks ran from 1947 until 1950, when Schulz quit after his editor refused to give him a raise from the $10 per comic he was making. After that, Schulz brought Li’l Folks to United Feature Syndicate. The national cartoon syndicator liked the comic, but needed to change its name because of a 1930s comic strip called Little Folks .

articles.title: This supernova impostor baffled astronomers for 15 years — until they found a hidden black hole feeding on an unstable star
articles.excerpt: A hidden black hole or neutron star companion to an unstable massive star is causing the system to erupt in light that mimics a supernova explosion.
articles.body: A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered. When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days.
